chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Basir said:

I asked one of the two Imams (peace be upon them both) about the purchase of the 'Gharar' (uncertainty/risk) and the 'Sariqah' (theft/uncertain goods), and he said: 'There is no prohibition except if it has mixed with it something else. As for the Sariqah itself, there is no prohibition except if it is from the property of the Sultan (ruler), in which case there is no harm with that.'

key_terms.السَّرِقَةِ: Al-Sariqah: Literally theft, but in fiqh often refers to goods stolen or goods with uncertain ownership/status.
key_terms.الْخِيَانَةِ: Al-Khiyanah: A type of commercial uncertainty or risk, often referring to buying goods where the quantity or quality is unknown.
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: La ba'sa: There is no harm (permissible).
key_terms.مَتَاعِ السُّلْطَانِ: Mat' al-Sultan: The property or goods of the ruler/government.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on buying stolen goods or goods with uncertainty (Gharar) according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between general uncertainty (*gharar*) in stolen goods and the specific exception of the Sultan’s property, reflecting the political and economic context of the time where state assets were treated differently. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that the nature of ownership and the potential for mixing with other goods (*ikhtilat*) determines the validity of the transaction, moving beyond a simple prohibition to a nuanced legal assessment.
